title: Static local variables
recap: A local variable normally has automatic duration, so a fresh object is created each time execution reaches its definition and destroyed when its block ends. Adding static gives a local variable static duration while preserving its block scope.

A static local is initialized once and retains its value between calls. This is useful for state that is truly unique to a function, such as a process-wide ID sequence, but hidden mutable state should not be used when callers need independent instances or a reset operation.
objectives: Give a block-scoped counter static duration.
Return the current ticket number before advancing the stored value.
Observe retained state through deterministic repeated calls.
warnings: Do not replace the static local with a global variable; that unnecessarily widens its scope.
Do not use a normal automatic local, which would restart the sequence on every call.
Use mutable static locals only for state that should be shared by every call and never independently reset.
challenge: Implement issueTicket() with an explicitly initialized static local unsigned int named s_nextTicket. Each call should return the current value and then advance the stored counter. Call it three times to print consecutive deterministic ticket numbers beginning at 100.
hints: Declare s_nextTicket inside issueTicket(), not at namespace scope.
Prefix the declaration with static so initialization happens only once.
Post-increment returns the old value before increasing the persistent counter.
